summary: BARA (Burning Activity Record Almanac; "bara" is Malay for ember) is a web app that turns 27 years of NASA FIRMS hotspots into one consistent burning calendar for the 11 ASEAN countries. MODIS and VIIRS count the same fires differently: across ASEAN, VIIRS reports 4.9 hotspots for every MODIS hotspot, so a raw record seems to jump in 2012. BARA converts every day since November 2000 into one unit, the VIIRS-equivalent hotspot, using a conversion factor learned separately for each 0.1 degree grid cell from the years both sensors flew. It then checks itself: on four years it never saw (2022-2025), its MODIS-based estimate misses the real VIIRS regional monthly total by 6.3% on average, while raw MODIS is 80% low. Users pick a country, a province, a drawn shape or coordinates and see a years-by-months calendar, whether the latest month and the current month to date are normal, the critical burning period, a day-by-day view, and downloadable CSV and PNG. This matters now: Suomi NPP left FIRMS in November 2026 and MODIS is due to stop in 2027. BARA keeps the long record meaningful for the responders, land managers and scientists who face each haze season.
details:
What it does
BARA is a web application that harmonizes NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspots into one consistent record for the 11 ASEAN countries, from November 2000 to 14 November 2026, and presents it as a burning activity calendar. A user chooses an area of interest (a country, a state or province, a drawn rectangle, polygon or circle, or a latitude and longitude with a radius) and immediately sees: a years-by-months calendar of hotspots with numbers and an accessible colour ramp; whether the latest month and the current month to date are below normal, near normal, above normal or extreme compared with the same period in every earlier year; the critical period (the three months that hold most of a normal year's burning); yearly totals; a seasonal profile; and a day-by-day view of any year. Everything can be downloaded as CSV (monthly table, grid-cell hotspot records, daily series), as a PNG, or shared as a link that reopens the exact view.

How it works
MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) count the same fires differently. Across ASEAN, VIIRS reports 4.9 hotspots for every MODIS hotspot, so a raw record seems to jump in 2012. BARA expresses every day in one unit, the VIIRS-equivalent hotspot. For each 0.1 degree grid cell it learns how many VIIRS hotspots correspond to one MODIS hotspot from 2012 to 2021, the years when both sensors flew. Cells with little data borrow from their neighbourhood. The factor ranges from 3.2 to 9.1 depending on place, which is why a single global multiplier fails. Each day uses the best sensor set that delivered data: Terra only (2000 to 2002), Terra and Aqua, Suomi NPP, and NOAA-20 for outages and after Suomi NPP left FIRMS in November 2026.

How we know it is valid
Four candidate models were scored by hiding each year from 2012 to 2021 in turn, and the simplest one that won was kept. The factors were then frozen and applied to 2022 to 2025, years the method never saw. The MODIS-based estimate missed the real VIIRS regional monthly total by 6.3% on average, with a bias of -1.6% and a correlation of 0.998, while raw MODIS is 80% low. For 2.5 degree areas the error is 16%. Values before 2012 are shown with a typical range, and the app has an evidence section that presents these results.

Benefits and intended impact
Early warning and emergency responders, land and peat managers, and scientists get a 27-year baseline that keeps its meaning when the sensor changes. This matters now, because Terra and Aqua MODIS are due to stop in 2027. An example from the app: in Central Kalimantan, October 2026 had 62,525 hotspots, 15 times a normal October, and August to October holds 91% of a normal year's burning.
What is creative
The harmonization is learned per place and per sensor set and is tested blind. The tool shows its own evidence and uncertainty to the user instead of hiding them. The same calendar can be switched to the raw sensors, which makes the 2012 artefact visible.

Tools
Python (Polars, NumPy, Shapely) for the data pipeline. GitHub Actions to fetch and grid 30.0 million NASA FIRMS detections in parallel. A static site (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet) on GitHub Pages, with no server and no login. Code: https://github.com/harithnabilf/bara

Factors considered
Accessibility: colour-blind safe and greyscale ramps, numbers in every cell, keyboard access. Honest limits: hotspots are not burned area, and cloud and smoke hide fires. Reliability: the map uses a bundled NASA Blue Marble image, so nothing depends on a live server. Reproducibility: the whole record can be rebuilt from NASA's servers.

AI use
The code, text, charts and slides were generated with an AI assistant (Claude), directed by the team. This is stated in the app, in the repository and on every slide.
